274.title: Without fear
274.hook: with no walls around the mind, there is no fear
274.howItsDone: The Heart Sutra is often chanted at Mahayana funerals, memorial services and bedsides, and many practitioners recite it when they're afraid, drawing on its line about a mind without walls.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was aprāptitva, and your line was nothing to get: the effort stays, and the grabbing drops.

A message sits unsent on the screen: an apology, or a no, put off for a week. The heart is loud. The hands are a little cold. Nothing in that message can hurt anyone. So what is the fear about? Look closer and there's often a wall being guarded. I'm the one who's never wrong. I'm the one who never lets people down. The fear stands at the wall like a guard at a gate, and the bigger the wall, the more guards it needs. Today's line from the Heart Sutra is only a few words long. With no walls, no fear.
screen: `A MESSAGE YOU HAVEN'T SENT.` → `A WALL BEING GUARDED.` → `FEAR AS THE GUARD.`

segments.voice: Because there was nothing to attain, the bodhisattva relied on wisdom. The sutra goes on: so the mind has no walls. And because there are no walls, there is no fear. Far beyond upside-down views, the bodhisattva reaches nirvana. The Sanskrit for walls is cittāvaraṇa. Citta, the mind. Āvaraṇa, a covering, an obstruction, something that closes in. In Xuanzang's Chinese, the word suggests being caught or snagged. What are the walls? Buddhist teachers say they're built from those upside-down views. The classic list has four: taking what changes for permanent, what can't satisfy for lasting happiness, what has no fixed self for a self, and what is unlovely for beautiful. Each wall is an idea about yourself and the world, held as if it were solid. Fear guards it. When wisdom sees that the wall is made of conditions, like everything else in this sutra, the guard has less to do. Two honest limits. First, the sutra is describing the bodhisattva, someone deep in wisdom. It doesn't promise that one reading switches fear off. Second, nothing here says to ignore real danger. The flinch that pulls your hand from a hot stove isn't a wall; it's your body doing its job. The fear the sutra points at is the kind that guards an idea. Name the wall, and very often the fear gets smaller, not because you fought it, but because you saw what it was protecting.
screen: `NO WALLS AROUND THE MIND.` · `CITTĀVARAṆA: A COVERING.` · `WALLS BUILT FROM UPSIDE-DOWN VIEWS.` · `FEAR GUARDS AN IDEA.` · then, large: `NO WALLS, NO FEAR.`

segments.voice: Let one small fear come to mind, a manageable one, not the biggest, and notice where it lives in the body: the chest, the stomach, the throat. Then ask quietly what wall it's guarding, what idea about you would crumble if it happened, and just name it. You don't have to knock it down; let the breath move around it, like air around a fence post.
Without fear. In the Heart Sutra, a mind with no walls around it has nothing for fear to guard.
Your line: no walls, no fear. Fewer walls, and fewer guards. Day two hundred seventy-four.

guess: no walls in the mind for fear to guard
bravely ignoring every danger you face
never feeling afraid of anything

pairs: what the walls are built from

myth: the Heart Sutra promises that one reading switches fear off
it describes the bodhisattva, someone deep in wisdom; it's a direction, not a switch.
the classic list of upside-down views has four
permanence, happiness, self and beauty, each seen where it isn't.
the sutra says to ignore real danger
the fear it points at guards an idea, not the flinch from a hot stove.

fork.setup: you've put off sending a hard message for a week and your heart pounds every time you open it. what does today's teaching suggest trying first?
options: name the idea about yourself the fear is guarding.
pretend the fear isn't there.
delete the message so the wall stays safe.
fork.reveal: the sutra links fear to walls around the mind; naming the wall is the first step to seeing it's made of conditions.

original.note: Sanskrit cittāvaraṇa: a covering or obstruction of the mind; the Heart Sutra says without it there is no fear.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'without fear' means Buddhists never feel afraid.
what it means: fear guards walls around the mind; when the walls are seen through, the guard has less to do.
what a scholar hears: the 'upside-down views' are the four viparyāsas, found in both Pali and Sanskrit sources, and the Chinese version pairs them with 'dream-thinking'.

275.title: Gate gate
275.hook: gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond, awakening, svaha
275.howItsDone: In Zen, Korean, Chinese, Vietnamese and Tibetan communities the Heart Sutra's mantra is chanted in its Sanskrit sound, or a local pronunciation of it, often repeated several times at the end of the sutra.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was without fear, and your line was no walls, no fear: name the wall, and the guard has less to do.

Gyatei, gyatei. Near the end of a Japanese morning service, the chanting speeds up and lands on these syllables. They aren't Japanese, and they aren't Chinese either. They're the last line of the Heart Sutra, and in the Chinese version East Asian temples chant, they were never translated. People chant the sound. After all the no's and all the emptiness, the sutra ends not with an argument but with something to say out loud.

Right after no walls and no fear, the sutra says: so know that the perfection of wisdom is the great mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the mantra that calms all suffering. Then it gives it, in Sanskrit: "gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā." Gate means gone. Pāragate, gone to the far shore, gone beyond. Pārasaṃgate, gone completely beyond, all the way over. Bodhi is awakening. And svāhā is an old ritual cry from Indian fire offerings, something like, so be it, or hail. Gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond, awakening, so be it. Scholars still argue about the grammar: gate might mean gone, or it might be calling out to someone, O you who have gone. Either way the picture is a crossing, the same far shore as the raft three days ago. Tradition explains the word mantra as man, the mind, and tra, a tool: a tool for the mind. It works less like a sentence you think about and more like a handrail you hold. Now the surprise. In the Chinese version tradition credits to the pilgrim and translator Xuanzang, every line is translated except this one. The mantra keeps its sound, written in Chinese characters used for their sound alone. That's why temples in Japan, Korea and Vietnam still chant a form of the old sounds, each in its own accent.
screen: `THE GREAT MANTRA.` · `GONE, GONE, GONE BEYOND.` · `A TOOL FOR THE MIND.` · `XUANZANG KEPT THE SOUND.` · then, large: `GONE BEYOND.`

segments.voice: If you'd like to, say the mantra softly three times, the way it's chanted: gate, gate, pāragate, pārasaṃgate, bodhi, svāhā, feeling the rhythm more than the meaning, with no worry about getting the sounds perfect. If you'd rather not say it, just listen to it inside. Then let the words go, and rest on the far shore of them, in the quiet after the sound.
Mantra. A tool for the mind: sounds held and repeated. The Heart Sutra ends with one, gone, gone, gone beyond.
Your line: gone beyond. A crossing you can say out loud, in any accent. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 275 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HEART IN YOUR DAY.`

fork.reveal: the mantra kept its sound in the Chinese, so East Asian Buddhists still chant a form of the Sanskrit sounds.

original.note: Sanskrit mantra: often explained as man (mind) + tra (tool), a tool for the mind.

what it means: a tool for the mind; the Heart Sutra ends by giving wisdom a sound to hold.
what a scholar hears: later sources credit Xuanzang with listing mantras among the 'five kinds of words not to translate', and 'gate' may be a feminine vocative addressed to wisdom herself.

sources.ref: Heart Sutra, 'the great mantra… that calms all suffering'

276.title: The Heart in your day
276.hook: Zen, Tibetan, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities chant it daily
276.howItsDone: Zen, Tibetan, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese Buddhist communities chant the Heart Sutra in daily services, often to the beat of a wooden fish drum, and in Japan many people copy it by hand as a practice called shakyō.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mantra, and your line was gone beyond: gate gate, the sound left untranslated. Today, the last day of the Heart Sutra.

Before sunrise at a Zen monastery in Japan, someone strikes a wooden drum shaped like a fish, and the monks start chanting at a steady, rolling clip. In a Korean temple, the same text, a different sound. In a Tibetan monastery, a longer version that opens on a mountain with the Buddha in meditation. In Vietnamese and Chinese temples from Taipei to Toronto, the same words at the morning service. For ten days you've read it one line at a time. People who chant it daily often know it by heart and get through it in a couple of minutes.
screen: `A WOODEN DRUM SHAPED LIKE A FISH.` → `KOREA, TIBET, VIETNAM, CHINA.` → `TWO MINUTES, BY HEART.`

segments.voice: The Heart Sutra is short enough to live with: one page. That's part of why it travels. In Japan, people copy it out by hand with a brush, character by character, a practice called shakyō, and temples collect the copies. It shows up on fans, on tea bowls, on scrolls in family altars. Tibetan Buddhists chant a longer version with a frame story: the Buddha sits in deep meditation on Vulture Peak while Avalokiteshvara and Shariputra talk, and at the end the Buddha comes out and says, well done. The name carries a double meaning. Hṛdaya in Sanskrit means heart, and also core, the essence. This is the heart of the huge Perfection of Wisdom literature, squeezed into one page. Now put the ten days back together. Prajnaparamita: wisdom gone beyond. Avalokiteshvara looked deep and saw the heaps were empty. Form is emptiness, emptiness is form: nothing stands alone. Emptiness is not nothing; the cup still holds tea. Not born, not destroyed. No eye, no ear: hold lists lightly. Nothing to attain. No walls, so no fear. And the mantra, gone beyond. If one line has to go with you, let it be the one this whole part turns on: form is emptiness. The chair, the phone, your own hands: real, useful, and made entirely of other things.
screen: `SHORT ENOUGH TO LIVE WITH.` · `COPIED BY HAND IN JAPAN.` · `HṚDAYA: HEART AND CORE.` · `TEN DAYS, ONE PAGE.` · then, large: `FORM IS EMPTINESS.`

segments.voice: If you have a copy of the Heart Sutra nearby, read it through once, slowly, aloud or silently, the way temples chant it at their morning services. If you don't, sit with its most famous line: on the in-breath, form is emptiness; on the out-breath, emptiness is form. Let your eyes rest on one ordinary object, a mug, a window, and see it as both.
Hṛdaya. Heart, and also core or essence in Sanskrit: the name for this one-page sutra, chanted daily across Asia and beyond.
Your line: form is emptiness. Ten days, one page, one line to keep. Until tomorrow.

guess: heart, and also core: the essence of something
love, the warm feeling you have for others
the life breath that keeps a body going

match.prompt: match each line of the Heart Sutra to what it meant.

it's called shakyō, and temples collect the copies.

fork.reveal: shakyō, hand-copying sutras with a brush, is a common practice in Japan, and temples collect the copies.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Heart Sutra is called that because it's about love.
what it means: heart as core: the essence of the Perfection of Wisdom teaching on one page.

what a scholar hears: the short and long versions differ mainly in the frame story, and some scholars argue the short text was first composed in Chinese and then rendered into Sanskrit, a view others dispute.

sources.ref: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita-hrdaya), short and long versions

277.title: What a koan is
277.hook: a short story or question Zen teachers use to stop the thinking mind
277.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen, and in Korean Seon through the hwadu, students work with a koan assigned by their teacher during sitting and daily life, and meet the teacher privately to show their understanding.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hṛdaya, heart and core, and your line was form is emptiness. That closed the Heart Sutra. Now a new part of the path: koans.

A monk asks a Zen teacher named Dongshan: what is Buddha? It's the biggest question a monk could ask. Dongshan answers: three pounds of flax. That's the whole story. If your mind did something just now, it may have gone looking for the trick. Maybe flax was what he was weighing at the time. Maybe it's a symbol. Maybe it's a joke. Notice that search: quick, clever, and a little desperate. For the next two weeks, you'll meet stories like this one. Zen teachers built a whole practice around them, and the first rule is a surprise.
screen: `WHAT IS BUDDHA?` → `THREE POUNDS OF FLAX.` → `THE MIND GOES LOOKING FOR THE TRICK.`

segments.voice: The word koan is Japanese. The Chinese is gong'an, and it originally meant a public case: the file on a legal case in a magistrate's court, a record other judges could look back on. Zen, called Chan in China, borrowed the word for records of encounters between early Chan teachers and their students. A question, an answer, sometimes a shout or a slap or a silence. Later teachers gathered them into collections with their own comments and verses. Two well-known ones are the Blue Cliff Record and the Gateless Gate, with forty-eight cases; Dongshan's three pounds of flax is case eighteen of the Gateless Gate. Here's what a koan is not: a riddle with a hidden answer at the back of the book. A student who brings the teacher a clever explanation is usually sent away. Teachers say the koan is meant to exhaust the thinking mind, the part that's always explaining, until something more direct shows up. They call the pressure that builds great doubt. In Korea, teachers work with a single phrase from a koan, called a hwadu, the head of the word, the point where words run out. So the first rule is: don't solve it. That doesn't mean ignore it. Hold it, turn it over, live with it, and let it work on you instead of you working on it.
screen: `GONG'AN: A PUBLIC CASE.` · `RECORDS OF ENCOUNTERS.` · `NOT A RIDDLE.` · `GREAT DOUBT.` · then, large: `DON'T SOLVE IT.`

segments.voice: Bring back today's koan: a monk asks, what is Buddha, and Dongshan says, three pounds of flax. Hold the words the way you'd hold a smooth stone in your palm, and when the mind starts explaining, notice it and come back to the words themselves. No answer needed; if the mind gets quiet, rest there, and if it gets restless, let that be part of it too.
Koan. From the Chinese gong'an, a public case: a record of a teacher's encounter, held in practice until the thinking mind lets go.
Your line: don't solve it. A koan is held, not cracked. Day two hundred seventy-seven, done.

guess: a teaching story held in practice, not solved
a Zen riddle with a clever hidden answer
a short poem chanted at the start of a sit

match.prompt: match each piece of today's teaching.

teachers usually send away students who bring a clever explanation.
the word first meant a case file in a Chinese court
gong'an: a public case, a record others could consult.

options: the teacher congratulates you and moves on.

fork.reveal: koans aren't solved by explanation; teachers look for a direct response, and a clever theory usually earns another round.

original.note: Japanese kōan, from Chinese gōng'àn: a public case, originally a court record.

trapdoor: what you thought: a koan is a Zen riddle.
what it means: a record of a real encounter, held in practice until thinking gives way to something more direct.
what a scholar hears: gong'an were magistrates' case files; the Song-dynasty collections, the Blue Cliff Record (1125) and the Gateless Gate (1228), turned Tang encounter stories into a curriculum.

278.title: Mu
278.hook: a monk asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has Buddha-nature; he answers "mu" (Gateless Gate 1)
278.carry: see what's there before you pick a side
278.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen and some Western Zen communities, 'mu' is often the first koan a teacher assigns; students breathe with it in sitting meditation and bring their response to private interviews with the teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday: koan, a public case you hold instead of crack, and your line, don't solve it.

Northern China, more than a thousand years ago. A stray dog wanders through a monastery courtyard. A monk watches it and turns to the old teacher Zhaozhou with a question he's clearly been saving. Does a dog have Buddha-nature, or not? The case doesn't say why he asks. But every monk there knew what the books said, so the question has a trap in it. Zhaozhou gives him one syllable. Wu. In Japanese, mu. It's the first case in the Gateless Gate, and for centuries it's been the first koan many Zen students are given.
screen: `A STRAY DOG IN THE COURTYARD.` → `DOES IT HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE?` → `ONE SYLLABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's why the answer is so strange. Mahayana sutras teach that all living beings have Buddha-nature, the capacity to wake up. So the textbook answer is yes. And mu means no. Or not, or without, or nothing. In one breath, it seems, Zhaozhou contradicted the scriptures. Argue that he meant no, and you're stuck. Argue that he meant yes, and you're stuck. Wumen, the monk who compiled the Gateless Gate in 1228, says in his comment that mu isn't the no of yes and no, and it isn't the nothing of being and nothing. Work on it with your whole body, he says, day and night, like someone who has swallowed a red-hot iron ball and can't spit it out. Tradition says Wumen himself worked on mu for six years. Here's a detail most people never hear. In another collection, the Book of Serenity, the same question comes to Zhaozhou on another day, and that time he answers: yes. Many teachers read it as a sign the answer was never the point; what mattered was what was happening in the person who asked. Zhaozhou, by tradition, lived to about one hundred twenty, teaching into extreme old age, famous for plain words that stopped people in their tracks. Mu is his most famous one. Students don't explain it. They become it, breath by breath.
screen: `ALL BEINGS HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE.` · `MU: NO, NOT, NOTHING.` · `A RED-HOT IRON BALL.` · `ON ANOTHER DAY, YES.` · then, large: `MU.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, let the sound mu go out with it, silently or as the softest hum, not thinking about what it means, just the sound riding the breath all the way out. When a thought comes, let the next mu follow it. If you'd like, imagine the sound filling the whole body, head to feet.
Mu. Zhaozhou's one-syllable answer about the dog: no, not, nothing, and none of those. The first koan of the Gateless Gate.
Your line: see what's there before you pick a side. Not the yes, not the no: mu. See you tomorrow.

guess: Zhaozhou's one-word reply that cuts off both yes and no
a sacred sound chanted to open every Zen sitting
a short Japanese word for a stray or homeless dog

match.prompt: match each piece of the first koan.

myth: Zhaozhou's 'mu' simply means dogs lack Buddha-nature
Wumen says it isn't the no of yes and no.
Mahayana sutras teach that all beings have Buddha-nature
that's why the monk's question was a trap.
in another collection Zhaozhou answers the same question with yes
the Book of Serenity records both answers.

fork.setup: you're Zhaozhou. a monk asks whether a dog has Buddha-nature, a question he already knows the textbook answer to. what do you say?
options: quote the sutra: yes, all beings have it.
give a long talk on Buddha-nature.
one syllable: mu.
fork.reveal: Zhaozhou said 'wu', mu in Japanese, which cut off both the textbook yes and any clever no.

original.note: Japanese mu, Chinese wú: no, not, without, nothing.

trapdoor: what you thought: mu means 'no', so the answer is no.
what it means: a word that cuts off both yes and no, held in practice rather than explained.

what a scholar hears: the 'yes' version is in the Book of Serenity, case 18, and Dahui Zonggao's huatou ('critical phrase') method in the twelfth century made 'wu' the favorite koan before Wumen placed it first.

sources.ref: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), case 1 and Wumen's comment

279.title: Wash your bowl
279.hook: a new monk asks for teaching; Zhaozhou: have you eaten? then wash your bowl (Gateless Gate 7)
279.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries meals are part of practice: in Japan monks eat with a set of nested ōryōki bowls in silence and clean them at their seats, and daily work (samu) such as washing and sweeping is treated as meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mu, Zhaozhou's one syllable, and your line, see what's there before you pick a side. Zhaozhou again today.
screen: `MU — SEE WHAT'S THERE BEFORE YOU PICK A SIDE.`

segments.voice: A monk arrives at Zhaozhou's monastery with the hunger of a first day. You may know it from a new job, a new school, a new team: wanting the real thing, the secret everyone else seems to know, wanting the orientation to end so the important part can start. He finds the old teacher and asks straight out: I've just entered the monastery. Please, teach me. He is ready for something big. The answer is the seventh case of the Gateless Gate, and it's about breakfast.
screen: `THE HUNGER OF A FIRST DAY.` → `WANTING THE REAL THING.` → `PLEASE, TEACH ME.`

segments.voice: Zhaozhou asks him: have you eaten your rice gruel? The monk says: I have. Zhaozhou says: then wash your bowl. And the story says the monk had an insight. That's the whole case. In a Chan monastery the morning meal was rice gruel, eaten from a monk's own bowl, which he washed himself. An ordinary moment of an ordinary day. The monk wanted the teaching somewhere else, later, bigger. Zhaozhou points him back to the bowl in front of him. Eat when you eat. Wash when you wash. The teaching isn't hiding behind daily life; it's in it. Wumen's verse on the case says something like this: it's so plain that it's hard to see, like searching for fire with a lit lantern in your hand. Had you known the fire was already there, your rice would have been cooked long ago. Teachers point to a second layer. Have you eaten can also mean: have you already had a taste of awakening? Then wash your bowl means: good, now don't carry it around. Clean up, even after insight. Don't make a trophy of it. In Japanese Zen monasteries today, meals still follow a careful form called ōryōki, with nested bowls that each monk cleans at the table and folds away in a cloth. The monk came for the secret. He got a chore. And the story says that was enough.
screen: `HAVE YOU EATEN?` · `THEN WASH YOUR BOWL.` · `FIRE IN THE LANTERN YOU CARRY.` · `CLEAN UP, EVEN AFTER INSIGHT.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR BOWL.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap and remember the last thing you ate from: the bowl or plate, the fork, the cup. Feel your hands, the hands that will wash it. Then just breathe, with nothing to seek beyond this room.
Ōryōki. The careful form for monastic meals in Japanese Zen, with nested bowls each monk washes and folds away: the ordinary task Zhaozhou pointed a monk back to.
Your line: clean up, even after insight. The teaching was in the bowl all along. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

a Japanese temple's daily rice-gruel breakfast dish
a monk's morning round, begging food door to door

pairs: have you eaten your rice gruel?

the case says the monk had an insight.
breakfast in a Chan monastery was rice gruel
and each monk washed his own bowl.
ōryōki is a way of eating with nested bowls in Japanese Zen

options: ask if he's eaten, then tell him to wash his bowl.

fork.reveal: Zhaozhou pointed him to the most ordinary task of the morning, and the story says the monk had an insight.

original.note: Chinese xǐ bōyú: wash (your) bowl, Zhaozhou's words in Gateless Gate case 7.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'wash your bowl' is a brush-off.
what it means: the teaching is in the ordinary task in front of you, even right after insight.
what a scholar hears: bōyú renders the Sanskrit pātra, the alms bowl, one of the few things a monk owns; 'have you eaten' is also an everyday greeting in Chinese.

sources.ref: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), case 7 and Wumen's verse

280.title: Baizhang's fox
280.hook: an old man was reborn a fox for saying the awakened are free of cause and effect (Gateless Gate 2)
280.howItsDone: Zen teachers use Baizhang's fox to warn students against thinking insight puts them beyond ethics and consequences; Baizhang himself is remembered for writing rules for monastic life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ōryōki, the nested bowls, and your line, clean up, even after insight. Today ends the week.

Every time the teacher Baizhang gave a talk, an old man stood at the back with the monks and listened. When the talk ended, he left with them. Nobody seemed to know him. One day, when everyone else had gone, the old man stayed behind. Baizhang asked: who are you? And the old man said: I'm not a human being. It's the second case of the Gateless Gate, and it reads like a ghost story. It's also about an old temptation in spiritual life: thinking you've gotten past the rules.
screen: `AN OLD MAN AT THE BACK.` → `WHO ARE YOU?` → `I'M NOT A HUMAN BEING.`

segments.voice: The old man tells his story. Long ago, in the time of a Buddha before ours, I lived on this mountain as its teacher. A student asked me: does a person of great practice still fall under cause and effect? I answered: no, they don't. For that answer I was reborn as a fox, five hundred lifetimes in a row. Please, give me a turning word, a phrase that can set me free. Baizhang said: they are not blind to cause and effect. In Chinese the difference is one character. The old man had said bù luò, doesn't fall into. Baizhang said bù mèi, isn't blind to, doesn't obscure. At that, the story says, the old man woke up. He bowed and asked Baizhang for a monk's funeral, behind the mountain. After the meal Baizhang called the monks to a funeral, and they were baffled, since no one was sick. He led them to a rock behind the mountain, drew out a dead fox with his staff, and cremated it with full rites. The old man thought awakening would lift him above cause and effect, the way some people imagine a spiritual person is beyond ordinary consequences. Baizhang's answer: no one is above it. Awakening means seeing it clearly. Look back at this week. No walls, no fear. Gone beyond. Form is emptiness. Don't solve it. Mu. Wash your bowl. And now: even the wisest are not blind to cause.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small cause and its effect from today: a late night and a heavy morning, a kind word and a softer face across the table. Look at it plainly, without blame, the way you'd watch one domino tip the next. Then watch the breath the same way, the in-breath leading to the out-breath, the out-breath making room for the next, link by link.
Baizhang's fox. An old teacher said the awakened don't fall under cause and effect, and lived five hundred lives as a fox until he heard: they aren't blind to it.
Your line: not blind to cause. Awake doesn't mean above it. Day two hundred eighty, and the week is whole.
